name: Measuring Whether Personalization Works
title: Measuring Whether Personalization Works
answer: Measuring whether personalization works means judging a tutoring or personalized learning tool by what students can do on their own, not by how often they log in. It matters because usage and enjoyment can rise while learning does not, and average results can hide groups who are falling behind. Schools should compare users with students who did not use it, check results more than once, and break results out by student group.

sections.body: Personalized learning is simple to describe but difficult to measure. Login counts and usage statistics only show that students used a tool, not that they learned from it. The pilot method described in Chapter 4 is especially relevant here, so a tutoring or personalized learning tool should be evaluated by the independent work students can produce, set against students who never used it. Motivation also deserves attention, but it can mislead because students often enjoy a new tool and that enjoyment can fade. Enjoyment is welcome, but it is not the same as learning.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a school compares students who use a tutoring or personalized learning tool with students who do not, looking at what each group can do independently. Results should be checked at the middle and end of the year, because a tool that helps in the first month may help less by spring and a tool that seems slow at first may pay off later. Checking at more than one point also lets teachers adjust how they use the tool. Results should also be broken out by student group, since an average gain can hide students who are falling further behind. The text gives one grade band for this work: a trial involved students in grades 7 through 9, where AI tools designed to support motivation and learning strategies were tested against a plain chatbot.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence for this idea is a trial with 371 students in grades 7 through 9, which found that AI tools designed to support motivation and learning strategies did not beat a plain chatbot on effort or knowledge (Futterer et al., 2026). The text also states that usage statistics show students logged in, not that they learned. The book does not give a separate evidence label for this idea beyond reporting that trial.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text: usage numbers can be mistaken for learning, and motivation can mislead because enjoyment of a new tool may fade. A single check can also mislead, since a tool may help less by spring or pay off later, so results should be checked at the middle and end of the year. An average gain can hide students who are falling further behind, so results should be broken out by student group. When results differ by group, the district should ask why and adjust, and the decisions about how to use or change the tool stay with teachers and district leaders. Personalized learning that helps only some students is not doing its job.
